name: Amdo Tibetan
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Amdo Tibetan is not in the catalog. The sweep list holds one item, Caplow's 2009 UCSB dissertation (607 pp.) on stress and Tibetan tonogenesis, which uses Rebkong Amdo as one of its two atonal source varieties; it is ProQuest-restricted (record opened, no abstract, no free copy; UCSB ADRL has no record; search engines and S2/OpenAlex/CORE/BASE/OATD were blocked or rate-limited from our machine), so it stays high-priority to acquire (Harvard HOLLIS link on file). The author's follow-up, Caplow 2016 LTBA 39(2) 'Reconstructing stress in Proto-Tibetan: Evidence from Balti and Rebkong Amdo' (not in the sweep list), gives the same data in a published form; only its abstract was reachable (paywalled at John Benjamins, OpenAlex closed), saved with the page HTML and OpenAlex record under with. That abstract is the best first-hand statement obtained: Rebkong Amdo disyllabic nouns/adjectives/numerals carry stress on the second (final) syllable; disyllabic verbs are never σ2-stressed and on limited data are σ1-stressed. On-disk secondary sources agree (Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 7.3.3, 9.5.6; Lim 2018 sec. 1.3.3.1; Caplow 2016 HL Balti paper fn. 3 gives Rebkong Amdo [xso.'ra] 'sickle'). Recommended acquisition: the 2016 LTBA full text (pp. 180-221) first, then the 2009 dissertation (pp. 527-528 per Lim for the reconstruction).

new_statements.quote: For both Balti and Rebkong Amdo, stress falls on the second syllable (σ2) of disyllabic non-verbs — nouns, adjectives, and numerals. [...] Disyllabic verbs are never stressed on σ2. For Balti, robust evidence shows that they are stressed on the first syllable (σ1). Limited data for Rebkong Amdo suggests the same pattern.

new_statements.locator: Abstract (p. 180); full text paywalled, only the publisher abstract page was opened
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. exists (1512 bytes, 09:23Z) and carries the abstract verbatim; the same text is present in the saved publisher page stripped HTML at char 2565-3100: "For both Balti and Rebkong Amdo, stress falls on the second syllable (σ2) of disyllabic non-verbs — nouns, adjectives, and numerals.... Disyllabic verbs are never stressed on σ2. For Balti, robust evidence shows that they are stressed on the first syllable (σ1). Limited data for Rebkong Amdo suggests the same pattern."), with header "Nancy J. Caplow... Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area, Volume 39, Issue 2, Jan 2016, p. 180-221, DOI 10.1075/ltba.39.2.01cap". The report's quote matches word for word (the [...] elision is marked)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In disyllabic non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, numerals) stress falls on the second syllable; disyllabic verbs are never stressed on the second syllable and (on limited data) carry first-syllable stress. Stress is a non-contrastive prosodic feature cued mainly by higher pitch; Amdo has no lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs: σ1, not σ2 (Caplow 2016 abstract, 'limited data'). Conflicting first-hand description for one migrant variety: Suzuki & Sonam Wangmo 2016: 105 (Shingnyag Tibetan, Lhagang) report stress 'on the first syllable of a polysyllabic word' as an often-prominent, non-distinctive prosodic feature. Suzuki 2017 (SAG7: 42) says it is not yet clear whether Amdo stress is distinctive or merely prosodic. Ebihara 2024: 6 (Gonghe nomad dialect) gives as an example pitch pattern 'first syllable low, second and later syllables high', non-distinctive, which is consistent with σ2 prominence in non-verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, disyllabic words in citation form; Caplow's abstract does not state the domain for longer words or phrases. All opened sources agree Amdo Tibetan is non-tonal (Makley et al. 1999: 112; Ebihara 2010: 43; Suzuki 2017 Table 1; Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 9.5.6) and that stress is not phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Caplow 2016) describes Rebkong (Reb gong / Tongren, Qinghai) Amdo, a core Kokonor-area variety within amdo1237 (no separate Glottolog code seen). The corroborating pedagogical description (Ebihara 2024) is the Gonghe County (Gyai village) nomad dialect, also amdo1237. The one conflicting first-hand statement (Suzuki & Sonam Wangmo 2016: first-syllable prominence) is for Shingnyag Tibetan, an Amdo-type migrant variety spoken in Lhagang, Kangding (Khams Minyag), also without its own Glottolog code.

new_statements.quote: For both Balti and Rebkong Amdo, stress falls on the second syllable (σ2) of disyllabic non-verbs — nouns, adjectives, and numerals. [...] Disyllabic verbs are never stressed on σ2. For Balti, robust evidence shows that they are stressed on the first syllable (σ1). Limited data for Rebkong Amdo suggests the same pattern. Thus σ1 stress is tentatively reconstructed for verbs in Proto-Tibetan.
new_statements.citation: Caplow, Nancy J. 2016. Reconstructing stress in Proto-Tibetan: Evidence from Balti and Rebkong Amdo. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 39(2): 180-221. DOI 10.1075/ltba.39.2.01cap
new_statements.locator: Abstract (publisher landing page https://www.jbe-platform.com/content/journals/10.1075/ltba.39.2.01cap, fetched sources 2026-09-17); full text paywalled
new_statements.reading: First-hand (author's own acoustic/perceptual study) statement for Rebkong Amdo Tibetan: in disyllabic nouns, adjectives and numerals stress is on the second = final syllable; disyllabic verbs are not final-stressed and, on limited data, are initial-stressed. So Amdo (Rebkong) has category-conditioned word stress: final in non-verbs, initial in verbs. This is an abstract-level statement, not the body text; the full data tables and any statement about longer words remain unread. Secondary corroboration on file: Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 7.3.3 and 9.5.6 (Amdo atonal; Caplow and others hold that Amdo has a stress opposition, secondary in the system) and Lim 2018 sec. 1.3.3.1 (summarising Caplow 2009: non-verbs *σσ́, verbs *σ́σ from Balti and Rebkong Amdo).

sources.note: p. 6 '声調はない': 'アムド・チベット語は…声調によって単語の意味の区別を行いません。単語ごとに，たとえば最初の音節を低く，2音節目以降を高く発音するなど，日本語のアクセントのような音の高低パターンがみられますが，これらには意味を弁別する機能はありません。' [No tone; word-level pitch patterns like Japanese accent, e.g. first syllable low and second and later syllables high, exist but do not distinguish meaning.] (page image verified)
